Reachability and collisions¶

We check which cubes the chisel can reach, how much it has to tilt, how tall the statue can be, and whether the hand and the chisel hit the cubes that are still there. The motion between cubes comes in the next notebook, with the controller.

Setup¶

In [1]:

panda = rtb.models.Panda()
cell = Cell()

1. Reach and tilt of the chisel¶

The table turns every cube to face the robot before it is carved. After that turn, two numbers are enough to know where the cube is for the arm: its distance $r$ from the axis of the table and its height $z$. So instead of checking every cube, we check each $(r, z)$ pair once.

For each pair we ask the inverse kinematics (ikine_LM, starting from qr) for a pose with the tip at the center of the cube. It uses random restarts, so we fix its seed to get the same poses in every run. The statue cubes are left out, since they are never carved.

In [2]:
voxels = proxy_pawn(STATUE_HEIGHT)

def slice_points(voxels) -> np.ndarray:
    """(r, z) of the marble cubes, one row per distinct point of the slice."""
    marble = voxels.centers[~voxels.is_statue]
    r = np.round(np.hypot(marble[:, 0], marble[:, 1]), 4)
    return np.unique(np.column_stack([r, np.round(marble[:, 2], 4)]), axis=0)


def reached(points: np.ndarray, tilt: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """Whether the tip reaches each (r, z) of the slice with the chisel tilted down by tilt."""
    x_T, _, z_T = cell.table_top.t
    ok = []
    for r, z in points:
        target = cell.tip_target(np.array([x_T - r, 0.0, z_T + z]), tilt) * cell.tip.inv()
        ok.append(panda.ikine_LM(target, q0=panda.qr, seed=IK_SEED).success)
    return np.array(ok)


points = slice_points(voxels)
tilts = [0, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45]
reach = {tilt: reached(points, np.deg2rad(tilt)) for tilt in tilts}
pd.DataFrame({"tilt [deg]": tilts, "reached": [reach[t].mean() for t in tilts]}).set_index("tilt [deg]").round(2)

30 1.00

In [3]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, tilt in zip(axes, [0, 30]):
    ok = reach[tilt]
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    ax.scatter(points[ok, 0], points[ok, 1] + cell.table_top.t[2], marker="s", s=60, color=REACHED, label="reached")
    ax.scatter(points[~ok, 0], points[~ok, 1] + cell.table_top.t[2], marker="s", s=60, color=MISSED, label="missed")
    ax.set_title(f"chisel tilted {tilt} deg down")
    ax.set_xlabel("distance from the axis of the table, r [m]")
axes[0].set_ylabel("height in the world, z [m]")
axes[0].legend(loc="lower left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

With a horizontal chisel the arm reaches 0.68 of the points, and the misses are a band in the middle of the block (left plot). Tilting the chisel down removes the band, and from 20 degrees on every point is reached. We use 30 degrees (APPROACH_TILT in src/sculptor/cell.py) to keep some margin.

2. Height of the statue¶

A taller statue needs a taller block, and the arm has to reach it and Swift has to draw it. In notebook 00, Swift handled the 1500 cubes of this size but not the 4950 small ones.

In [4]:
heights: list[float] = [0.42, 0.54, 0.66, 0.78]
rows: list = []
for h in heights:
    v = proxy_pawn(h)
    rows.append({"height [m]": h, "reached": reached(slice_points(v), APPROACH_TILT).mean(), "cubes": len(v.centers)})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("height [m]").round(2)

reached cubes
height [m]
0.42 1.00 1815

The arm reaches every point up to 0.54 m and starts to miss at 0.66 m (0.99), so the arm does not limit the statue. The 0.42 m block has 1815 cubes, close to the 1500 of notebook 00, while the 0.54 m one has 3211. We use 0.42 m (STATUE_HEIGHT in src/sculptor/model.py).

3. Hitboxes¶

To check whether the hand or the chisel hits the block, we cover them with spheres (hitboxes) that Swift does not draw. A sphere is the easiest shape to test against a cube. We take the point $\mathbf{p}$ of the cube closest to the center $\mathbf{c}$ of the sphere, and the sphere touches the cube when that point is nearer than the radius $r$. The cubes are not rotated in the block frame, so $\mathbf{p}$ is just $\mathbf{c}$ clamped between the two opposite corners of the cube, one coordinate at a time:

$$\mathbf{p} = \mathrm{clip}(\mathbf{c},\ \mathbf{b}_{\min},\ \mathbf{b}_{\max}), \qquad \text{touch if } \lVert \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c} \rVert < r$$

If the center is inside the cube, $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{c}$ and the distance is 0.

The toolbox already gives the Panda simple collision shapes, spheres and cylinders. Each cylinder of radius $r$ becomes a row of spheres along its axis, $d = r/2$ apart, and so does the chisel, as wide as the base of its tip. Halfway between two neighbours the surface of the cylinder is a bit farther than $r$ from both centers, so the spheres get a slightly bigger radius, the distance to that point:

$$r' = \sqrt{r^2 + (d/2)^2} = r\sqrt{1 + 1/16}$$

On top of that, every sphere is 3 mm bigger than what Swift draws, as a safety margin.

In [5]:
hitboxes = Hitboxes(panda, cell)
_, radii = hitboxes.world(panda.qr)
print(f"Radius of the chisel spheres: {radii[-1] * 1000:.1f} mm")
pd.Series(hitboxes.count, name="spheres").to_frame()

Radius of the chisel spheres: 10.8 mm

4. Collisions and carving order¶

Whether the chisel hits a cube depends on which cubes are still there, so it depends on the order of the carving. We go through the marble cubes in order. For each one the table turns it to the robot, the arm takes its pose (the IK starts from the previous pose, as in the real carving), and we check the hitboxes against the cubes not removed yet. The target cube is left out, since the point of the chisel is meant to be inside it.

In [6]:
order = carving_order(voxels, n_sides=None)
phi = table_angles(voxels, order, cell, n_sides=None)
q = solve_poses(panda, cell, voxels, order, phi, seed=IK_SEED)

# The point of the tip must be inside its own target cube
for i, angle, q_i in zip(order, phi, q):
    tip_B = cell.world_to_block(panda.fkine(q_i, tool=cell.tip).t, angle)[0]
    assert cube_at(tip_B, voxels.centers, voxels.size) == i

reverse, phi_reverse = order[::-1], phi[::-1]
q_reverse = solve_poses(panda, cell, voxels, reverse, phi_reverse, seed=IK_SEED)
pd.DataFrame({"order": ["top down, outside in", "bottom up, inside out"],
              "blocked": [len(hitboxes.blocked(voxels, order, phi, q)),
                          len(hitboxes.blocked(voxels, reverse, phi_reverse, q_reverse))],
              "marble cubes": len(order)}).set_index("order")

In [7]:
# Where the blocked cubes are
stuck = hitboxes.blocked(voxels, order, phi, q)
r = np.hypot(voxels.centers[stuck, 0], voxels.centers[stuck, 1])
pd.DataFrame({"r [m]": r, "z [m]": voxels.centers[stuck, 2]}).round(3).value_counts().to_frame("cubes")
Out[7]:
cubes
r [m] z [m]
0.06 0.315 4
0.225 4

In our order (top layer first, outside in) only 8 of the 1605 marble cubes are blocked, against 1589 in the reverse order (carving_order in src/sculptor/carving.py). The 8 blocked cubes are at $r = 0.06$ m, four at $z = 0.225$ m and four at $z = 0.315$ m, which is the marble under the collar and under the head of the pawn. A chisel coming from above would have to go through the statue to reach them, so they stay. A second tilt could remove them, but we leave it out.

5. Size of the hitboxes¶

The 3 mm margin is our choice, so we change the size of the spheres and see whether the result changes. The spheres of the arm and the hand are scaled, and an extra margin is added to all of them.

In [8]:
rows = [{"change": f"arm and hand x{s}", "blocked": len(hitboxes.blocked(voxels, order, phi, q, arm_scale=s))} for s in [0.5, 1.0, 1.5]]
rows += [{"change": f"extra margin {m * 1000:.0f} mm", "blocked": len(hitboxes.blocked(voxels, order, phi, q, extra=m))}
         for m in [0.001, 0.002, 0.003, 0.004, 0.005]]
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("change")
Out[8]:
blocked
change
arm and hand x0.5 8
arm and hand x1.0 8
arm and hand x1.5 8
extra margin 1 mm 8
extra margin 2 mm 8
extra margin 3 mm 8
extra margin 4 mm 36
extra margin 5 mm 1605

Making the spheres of the arm and the hand half or 1.5 times as big changes nothing, because they never get close to the block, so it does not matter that the collision shapes of the Panda are only approximate. The chisel is what matters. With up to 3 mm of extra margin the result stays the same, at 4 mm 36 cubes are blocked and at 5 mm all of them. The chisel spheres have a radius of 10.8 mm (section 3), and a few millimetres more make the sphere at the point reach the cubes next to its target.

6. Scene in Swift¶

The arm at the poses of the carving order, with the collision shapes of the Panda drawn see-through. In the top layer the arm goes cube by cube and removes the cube under the tip. Then it jumps 160 cubes at a time, and the cubes in between disappear at once, so the GIF gets to the base of the pawn quickly. Here the arm jumps between poses; the real motion comes with the controller in the next notebook.

In [9]:
GIF = RECORDINGS / "03_reachability_poses.gif"
STEP_EVERY = 160

if RECORD or not GIF.exists():
    env = swift.Swift()
    env.launch(realtime=True, browser=None)
    panda.q = panda.qr
    env.add(panda, collision_alpha=0.35)
    add_table(env, cell)
    cubes, ids = add_block(env, voxels, cell)
    chisel = add_chisel(env, panda.fkine(panda.q, tool=cell.tip))
    env.step(0.05)

    def show_pose(k: int) -> None:
        place_block(cubes, voxels, cell, phi[k])
        panda.q = q[k]
        place_chisel(chisel, panda.fkine(q[k], tool=cell.tip))

    n_top = int(np.sum(voxels.centers[order, 2] == voxels.centers[order[0], 2]))
    with recording(env, GIF):
        # The top layer, one cube at a time
        for k in range(n_top):
            show_pose(k)
            env.step(0.05)
            env.remove(ids[order[k]])
            env.step(0.05)
        # The rest in jumps; the cubes in between disappear at once
        done = n_top
        for k in range(n_top, len(order), STEP_EVERY):
            for i in order[done:k]:
                env.remove(ids[i])
            done = k
            show_pose(k)
            for _ in range(8):
                env.step(0.05)
    env.close()

show_gif(GIF)
Out[9]:

Summary¶

The next notebooks reuse the tilt of the chisel (APPROACH_TILT), Cell.tip_target and Cell.facing_angle from src/sculptor/cell.py, the height of the statue (STATUE_HEIGHT) from src/sculptor/model.py, the carving order (carving_order) from src/sculptor/carving.py and the hitboxes from src/sculptor/collision.py.

A horizontal chisel misses a band in the middle of the block, and tilted 30 degrees down it reaches all of it (section 1). The arm reaches blocks up to 0.54 m, so the height of 0.42 m comes from what Swift can draw (section 2).

In our order 8 of the 1605 marble cubes are blocked, all under the collar and the head, against 1589 in the reverse order (section 4). The size of the chisel spheres decides this, the size of the arm spheres does not, and there is room for 3 mm more margin (section 5). This check only looks at the final pose for each cube; the next notebook checks the motion.
